title: Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top
question: How much assessment money does the City collect and pass to each benefit or improvement district, and how much does the City then grant the same organization from its own budget?
finding: The payment file shows 19 district organizations that received assessments collected by the City, $498.9 million since fiscal 2019 ($228.7 million of it to the tourism district paid by hotels); the City’s own list names 16 community benefit districts. On top of the assessments the City paid the same organizations $69.7 million in grants. For the neighbourhood districts grants rose from $11.9 million in fiscal 2019–2022 to $36.5 million in fiscal 2023–2026. In 5 districts City grants in the later years came to half or more of the assessment itself: Excelsior Action Group (205%); No Of Market/Tenderloin Com Benefit Corp (106%); Castro Upper Market Cmnty Benefit Dist (66%); Fisherman's Wharf Association Of SF (62%); Noe Valley Association (55%). Organizations the files tie to a district were paid a further $18.7 million (San Francisco Travel Association ($13.0 million); Union Square Foundation ($5.6 million); Ingleside Community Fund ($119,300)).
how: A district organization is a payee that received $100,000 or more from the account through which the Treasurer and the general City accounts hand over assessments held for others (“Other Obligations-Agency Fund”) and whose name reads as a district or its owners’ association. Assessments are those payments; City grants are payments to the same payee on City grant lines; other payments are everything else (rent, contracts). Later-years share is grants divided by assessments for fiscal 2023 to 2026. Related organizations are names the project’s owner-groups tie to the district on record evidence (a related-organization schedule or the same business account) and that the City also pays. A payment is dated by its voucher number.
limits: On assessment districts: the Board’s files record each one being formed or renewed by resolution, with assessment ballots cast for the parcels assessed, the City collects the assessment and passes it to the district’s organization, which files a tax return as a private nonprofit. The grants have a plain purpose: the largest are titled, as keyed, “ECN Downtown Ambassador”, “PRT-EX-Pop-Up Events”, “Tenderloin Clean WFD” and “ECN Tenderloin Healthy Spaces”. The question a grant on top raises is narrower: a district’s board answers to the owners who pay the assessment, so a grant made without competition goes to a body the City does not control. How each grant was awarded is in the exceptions and winners files. What would settle it: each district’s management agreement with the City and the annual reports that the Board’s files say each district must submit under it. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.
